title: What are @NamedQuery and @NamedNativeQuery in JPA? How do they differ from an inline @Query, and why are they validated at startup?

s1_definition.profdef: `@NamedQuery` defines a reusable **JPQL** query with a name, declared on the entity (or in orm.xml), that the persistence provider **parses and validates once at application startup** and caches, so it is "pre-compiled" and fails fast if the JPQL is invalid. `@NamedNativeQuery` is the same idea for a **native SQL** query. An inline `@Query` on a Spring Data repository method is also typically validated at startup for JPQL, but named queries are centrally declared on the entity, reusable across repositories and the `EntityManager`, and are the JPA-standard way to register queries by name. You invoke a named query by its name via `em.createNamedQuery("Account.findActive")` or by convention from a Spring Data method.
s1_definition.analogy: A named query is like a pre-approved, pre-printed standard form kept in the bank's forms cabinet — it was checked by compliance once when it was added, so every teller who pulls it knows it is valid, and they just fill in the blanks (parameters). An inline query is like a teller writing out a request freehand on their own desk each time; convenient and local, but the standard named form is the official, reusable, pre-validated one. Validating at startup is compliance checking every form in the cabinet the moment the branch opens, so a broken form is caught before any customer is served, not in the middle of a transaction.
s1_definition.oneliner: @NamedQuery (JPQL) and @NamedNativeQuery (SQL) are named, reusable, startup-validated queries declared on the entity; inline @Query is local to a repository method but also usually validated at startup.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@NamedQuery` defines a reusable **JPQL** query with a name, declared on the entity (or in orm.xml), that the persistence provider **parses and validates once at application startup** and caches, so it is "pre-compiled" and fails fast if the JPQL is invalid. `@NamedNativeQuery` is the same idea for a **native SQL** query. An inline `@Query` on a Spring Data repository method is also typically validated at startup for JPQL, but named queries are centrally declared on the entity, reusable across repositories and the `EntityManager`, and are the JPA-standard way to register queries by name. You invoke a named query by its name via `em.createNamedQuery("Account.findActive")` or by convention from a Spring Data method.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A named query is like a pre-approved, pre-printed standard form kept in the bank's forms cabinet — it was checked by compliance once when it was added, so every teller who pulls it knows it is valid, and they just fill in the blanks (parameters). An inline query is like a teller writing out a request freehand on their own desk each time; convenient and local, but the standard named form is the official, reusable, pre-validated one. Validating at startup is compliance checking every form in the cabinet the moment the branch opens, so a broken form is caught before any customer is served, not in the middle of a transaction.

**One line to remember:** @NamedQuery (JPQL) and @NamedNativeQuery (SQL) are named, reusable, startup-validated queries declared on the entity; inline @Query is local to a repository method but also usually validated at startup.

sections.s2_technical:
A named query is registered with a unique name and its query text. The convention is to prefix with the entity name, like `Account.findByStatus`. The provider parses it once at bootstrap: for JPQL it validates the syntax, the entity and field names, and the parameter usage; if anything is wrong the application fails to start with a clear error. This "fail fast at startup" is the main safety benefit — you never ship a broken JPQL query that only blows up at runtime when a user hits that path.

```java
@Entity
@NamedQuery(
    name = "Account.findActiveByType",
    query = "select a from Account a where a.status = 'ACTIVE' and a.type = :type")
@NamedNativeQuery(
    name = "Account.rawBalanceSum",
    query = "SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'")
public class Account { ... }
```

You invoke them by name:

```java
List<Account> active = em.createNamedQuery("Account.findActiveByType", Account.class)
    .setParameter("type", "SAVINGS").getResultList();
```

With Spring Data, if a repository method name matches a declared named query (entity name + method name), Spring uses it automatically; or you reference it explicitly. An inline `@Query("select a from Account a where ...")` on a repository method achieves the same querying but the query text lives next to the method. For JPQL, Spring Data also validates `@Query` JPQL at startup by default. The real differences: named queries are declared centrally on the entity and are reusable from multiple repositories and from the raw `EntityManager`, follow the JPA standard, and keep query text out of repository interfaces; inline `@Query` is more local and discoverable right at the method but is not reusable elsewhere by name.

For native queries, both `@NamedNativeQuery` and `@Query(nativeQuery = true)` exist. Native SQL is **not** validated for correctness at startup the way JPQL is, because the provider does not parse vendor SQL — so a broken native query still fails at runtime. Named native queries often pair with `@SqlResultSetMapping` to map arbitrary result columns to entities or DTOs.

Senior nuances: named queries can be overridden in orm.xml without recompiling, which is useful for tuning in production. JPQL named queries are database-portable; named native queries are not. Keep query text out of business logic by naming and reusing. And a subtle gotcha: a `@NamedQuery` and an inline `@Query` with the same effective name can conflict — be deliberate about naming.
sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — a typo in a JPQL query reached production and failed only when a user hit that screen.** At National Bank of India, an inline query referenced a misspelled field, compiled fine, and threw at runtime weeks later. Moving it to a `@NamedQuery` meant the provider validated it at startup and the app would refuse to boot with the typo. This is exactly the startup-validation benefit.

**Problem 2 — the same "active accounts by type" query was duplicated in three repositories.** The identical JPQL was copy-pasted and drifted. Declaring it once as a `@NamedQuery` on the entity made it reusable from every repository and the EntityManager. This is exactly the reuse benefit.

What the code will do: an `Account` entity declaring a `@NamedQuery` (JPQL) and a `@NamedNativeQuery` (SQL with a result-set mapping), a repository using the named query by convention, and a service calling both plus an inline `@Query` for contrast.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build (a typo in a @NamedQuery would FAIL this boot step)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/named-query-service-1.0.0.jar

# Call the named JPQL query
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/active-savings
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: fetch active savings accounts, then summarize active balance by type.

Step 1 — at application startup, the provider parses `Account.findActiveByType` as JPQL, checks that Account and its status and type fields exist, and validates the named parameter. If there were a typo, the application would refuse to boot with a clear error — that is the pre-compilation safety.

Step 2 — the repository method `findActiveByType("SAVINGS")` matches the named query by convention, so Spring binds the type parameter and runs the cached, validated query, returning the savings account.

Step 3 — `balanceByType` calls the `@NamedNativeQuery` by name. This runs raw SQL grouping by type and summing balances. Native SQL is not JPQL-validated at startup, so a SQL error here would surface at runtime, not boot.

Step 4 — the native result columns (type, totalBalance) are mapped by `@SqlResultSetMapping` into the BalanceSummary DTO via its constructor.

Step 5 — the service returns typed results. The named JPQL query is reusable from any repository or the EntityManager, unlike the inline `@Query` which is local to its method.

```
2026-10-24 01:26:30 DEBUG Hibernate: select a.* from accounts a where a.status='ACTIVE' and a.type=?
2026-10-24 01:26:31 DEBUG Hibernate: SELECT type, SUM(balance) FROM accounts WHERE status='ACTIVE' GROUP BY type
2026-10-24 01:26:31 INFO  Native named query returned 2 summary rows
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  APP STARTUP
    │  parse & validate @NamedQuery (JPQL) → typo? FAIL BOOT fail-fast
    │  register @NamedNativeQuery (SQL, NOT parsed) + @SqlResultSetMapping
    ▼
  RUNTIME
    │
    ├─ findActiveByType("SAVINGS")
    │    └→ cached named JPQL → WHERE status='ACTIVE' AND type=? → List<Account>
    │
    └─ createNamedQuery("Account.sumActiveBalanceByType")
         └→ native SQL GROUP BY type → columns → ConstructorResult → BalanceSummary DTO
  (inline @Query: local to method, JPQL validated at startup, not reusable by name)
```

  ┌──────────┐ REST ┌────────────────────────┐ JDBC ┌────────────┐
  │ Reporting│─────→│ Account Query Service  │─────→│ PostgreSQL │
  │ UI       │      │ named JPQL + native     │      │ accounts   │

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — @NamedQuery vs inline @Query (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Registry/Catalog: named queries kept centrally on entity   │
  │  DTO projection via @SqlResultSetMapping                     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: entity owns its query catalog; repo exposes access      │
  │  O: tune a named query in orm.xml without recompiling       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Comparison (as prose) ──
  @NamedQuery (JPQL): named, central on entity, reusable everywhere,
     PARSED+VALIDATED at startup (fail fast), portable across databases.
  @NamedNativeQuery (SQL): named native; NOT JPQL-validated at startup;
     pairs with @SqlResultSetMapping; not portable.
  inline @Query: local to repo method, discoverable, JPQL validated at
     startup by Spring Data, but not reusable by name elsewhere.

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. startup → validate named JPQL (typo → boot fails)
  2. repo.findActiveByType → cached named query → List<Account>
  3. em.createNamedQuery(native) → SQL → ConstructorResult → DTO

  (Caution) native queries fail at runtime, not boot. (Caution) name clashes between
     @NamedQuery and @Query. Rule: central reusable → named; local one-off → inline.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A named query defines a reusable JPQL query with a name, declared on the entity or in the orm mapping file, and the persistence provider parses and validates it once at application startup and caches it, which is why people call it pre-compiled. The big safety benefit is that if the JPQL has a typo, references a field that does not exist, or misuses a parameter, the application fails fast at boot with a clear error instead of shipping a broken query that only explodes at runtime when a user finally hits that path. The named native query is the same idea for raw SQL, and it usually pairs with a result-set mapping that maps the arbitrary result columns into an entity or a DTO through a constructor.

The difference from an inline query on a Spring Data repository method is mostly about location and reuse. A named query is declared centrally on the entity and can be invoked by name from multiple repositories and from the raw entity manager, it follows the JPA standard, and it keeps query text out of the repository interfaces. An inline query keeps the text right next to the method, which is discoverable and convenient, and Spring Data also validates inline JPQL at startup, but it is local and not reusable elsewhere by name. One important caveat is that native SQL, whether named or inline, is not validated for correctness at startup because the provider does not parse vendor SQL, so a broken native query still fails at runtime.

At National Bank of India both benefits were concrete. We once shipped an inline JPQL query with a misspelled field name that compiled fine and only threw weeks later when a user opened that screen, and after moving it to a named query the application would have refused to boot with the typo, catching it in the build. We also had the same active-accounts-by-type query copy-pasted into three repositories where it had started to drift, so I declared it once as a named query on the entity and reused it everywhere. The nuances I always mention are that JPQL named queries are database portable while named native queries are not, that named queries can be overridden in the orm mapping file to tune them in production without recompiling, and that I am deliberate about names so a named query and an inline query do not clash.

---

keyPoints: Defined on entity class — pre-compiled, validated at startup
@NamedQuery: JPQL, catches syntax errors at boot time (fail-fast)
Modern alternative: @Query on repository method — same validation, better location
